a: The poorest of the people and the most worthless of the slaves came forward to betray their rich masters
p: Tacitus's city of informers is background to Jesus's warning that people will hand each other over.
b: Background only. After the fighting, Tacitus says slaves informed on masters and friends on friends. Jesus warned his followers of the same kind of betrayal in hard times: "One brother will hand another over to be killed, and a father will hand over his child" (Matthew 10:21), and "People will hand each other over and hate each other" (Matthew 24:10). Tacitus is not describing Christians, and the Gospels are not describing Rome's civil war. The link is only that both name the first wound of a society at war with itself: trust breaks. For slaves in the Bible's world see the topic Slavery in the Bible.

a: Domitian had taken the name of Caesar
p: Vespasian's younger son, who appears in almost every part of this book, and who was later emperor.
b: Domitian was Vespasian's younger son. Tacitus says he took the name of Caesar and moved into the Caesars' house but did not yet work at ruling. Suetonius agrees that once Vitellius was beaten Domitian was hailed as Caesar and took the city praetorship with a consul's powers "only in name" (Domitian 1.3), and that during the fighting he had been in the Capitol and slipped out disguised as a follower of Isis (Domitian 1.2). Josephus also has Domitian escape from the Capitol, and has Mucianus present him to the crowd until his father came (War 4.11.4). Many readers place the book of Revelation in Domitian's reign; see the topic When Was Revelation Written?

a: Arrius Varus held the command of the Praetorian Guard
p: The emperor's own soldiers in Rome, and a word Paul uses in a letter from prison.
b: The Praetorian Guard was the body of soldiers kept in Rome to protect the emperor. Its commander was the "praetorian prefect"; Tacitus's Latin is praefectura praetorii. Paul wrote that his chains were seen for what they were "by the whole praetorium and by everyone else" (Philippians 1:13) and sent greetings from "those who belong to Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22). The site's Philippians page asks where Paul wrote from (Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea) and reads "praetorium and everyone else" as people, not a building. If the letter is from Rome, this guard is one of the groups Paul means.

a: The civil war had begun in Gaul and Spain, then drawn in Germany and then Illyricum, and had swept through Egypt, Judea, Syria and every province and army.
t: The war that reached Judea, Syria and Illyricum
p: Tacitus counts the Jewish war inside Rome's civil war. Several of his provinces are places in Acts and Romans.
b: Tacitus lists the provinces the civil war crossed and puts Judea among them. Josephus joins the two wars as well: the old oracle that "one from their country should become governor of the habitable earth" "certainly denoted the government of Vespasian, who was appointed emperor in Judea" (War 6.5.4), and Vespasian first made sure of Egypt, because Egypt fed Rome (War 4.10.5). Other names here are Bible places. Syria is where Quirinius governed (Luke 2:2). Paul planned to go to Spain (Romans 15:24; Romans 15:28) and preached "as far as Illyricum" (Romans 15:19). Jesus said of hard times to come, "You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars" (Matthew 24:6). Whether that speaks of AD 70, of the end, or of both is argued on the site's Matthew pages.

a: Lucilius Bassus was sent with some light cavalry to bring order to Campania
p: Josephus has a Lucilius Bassus take over the Jewish war after Titus. Is he the same man? Likely.
b: Tacitus first names this Lucilius Bassus as a cavalry commander who became prefect of the fleets at Ravenna and Misenum under Vitellius (2:100), then turned the Ravenna fleet to Vespasian (3:12; 3:36). Josephus has "Lucilius Bassus" sent "as legate into Judea" after Titus left, where he "received the army from Cerealis Vitellianus, and took that citadel which was in Herodium" (War 7.6.1). Same person? Likely. The name, the rank (a commander who held the fleets, then a legate), the date and his service to Vespasian all fit, and Bassus leaves Italy's story here. Neither Tacitus nor Josephus says outright that they are one man, and Wikipedia's article on Lucilius Bassus treats them as one without giving an argument. Josephus says Herod built the fortress Herodium and named it after himself (War 1.21.10); Matthew names Herod only as the king when Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1).

a: Mucianus had also sent some letters to the Senate
p: The man who ran Rome for Vespasian was governor of Syria. Josephus shows him meeting Vespasian.
b: Mucianus governed Syria. Josephus says that when Vespasian came to Berytus, "Mucianus came also, who was the president of the province" (War 4.10.6). Vespasian sent him to Italy with an army, and because it was winter he marched by land "through Cappadocia and Phrygia" (War 4.11.1); the Jews at Pentecost named both lands among the places they came from (Acts 2:9-10). Dio says that while Vespasian was in Egypt, Mucianus ran affairs with Domitian and "plumed himself greatly upon his honours" (65.2). That is the Mucianus Tacitus shows here: a governor of the East who has become the real power in Rome.

a: a triumph for a civil war, though the excuse was an expedition against the Sarmatae
t: A triumph, and Paul's victory parade
p: A Roman triumph was a victory parade. Paul uses the picture twice for Christ.
b: A triumph was the parade of a victorious general through Rome, and the Senate could not honestly vote one for beating Romans, so the Sarmatae (a people north of the Danube) were the excuse. Paul takes the picture for Christ: God "always leads us in his victory parade in Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:14), and Christ led "the rulers and the authorities" "in his victory parade" (Colossians 2:15). The Flavian triumph that Josephus describes was over the Jews. It ended at the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, where the procession waited until word came that the enemy general Simon had been put to death (War 7.5.6).

a: those teachers of philosophy who hold that nothing is good but what is honorable
t: Stoics at Rome and Stoics at Athens
p: Helvidius followed the Stoics, the school Paul met in Athens. They say virtue is the only good.
b: Tacitus does not name the school here; these teachers are the Stoics, and Wikipedia calls Helvidius Priscus a Stoic. Luke tells that when Paul spoke in Athens, "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also took him on" (Acts 17:18). Partly differs. The Stoic teachers Tacitus describes would not call wealth or rank good or bad. The Bible's wisdom books treat riches as something God can give: "when God gives any person riches and property and lets him be master of them... this is God's gift" (Ecclesiastes 5:19). Even so, Tacitus's picture of a man who "wasn't shaken by danger" and held to what was right is one the Bible also honors in its prophets, who spoke truth to kings.

a: Helvidius Priscus came from the town of Cluviae
p: A senator of modest family who became the Senate's loudest voice for free speech under Vespasian.
b: Tacitus gives Helvidius a short life story here, because he is "a man I'll have to speak of often". His father had risen from the ranks to the top centurion's post. He married the daughter of Thrasea Paetus, a Stoic senator whom Nero killed. Tacitus says that after Thrasea's fall Helvidius was driven into exile (4:6; in Annals 16.33 he is expelled from Italy), that he moved that the Capitol be rebuilt with public money (4:9), and that as praetor he led the rite that purified its site (4:53). Suetonius says Vespasian banished him and later ordered his death, then sent to recall the men sent to kill him, but a false report said he was already dead (Vespasian 15). The surviving Histories stops at 5:26, before that end.

a: Marcellus demanded the urn (drawing lots)
p: Marcellus wants the envoys chosen by lot. The apostles chose Matthias the same way.
b: Marcellus wants the envoys drawn by lot so no one can scheme or take offense. The Latin has urnam (4:6), the urn, and sorte et urna (4:7), "by lot and urn". Lots were a common way to pick people for hard or honored jobs. The apostles used them: "They handed out lots for them. The lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted in with the eleven apostles" (Acts 1:26). Agrees on the method, differs on who decides. For Marcellus a lot is a fair accident. Proverbs says "People throw the lot into the lap, but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33).

a: while I pray for good emperors, I can put up with whatever kind we get
t: Pray for rulers, put up with rulers
p: Marcellus's rule for living under any emperor sounds like Paul's, but the reasons differ.
b: Marcellus, who had served Nero, speaks as a survivor. The Bible asks for something like it: "make requests, prayers, appeals and thanksgivings for every person, for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:1-2), and "Submit to the king as the one ranked highest" (1 Peter 2:13). Paul's longest word is Romans 13:1-7. Agrees in the outward duty; differs in the ground and the limit. Marcellus obeys from caution (he says friendship with Nero was as nerve-racking as exile). Paul obeys "for the sake of conscience" (Romans 13:5), and the apostles draw a line: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Helvidius answers Marcellus (4:7), and Montanus will answer him again (4:42).

a: Musonius Rufus attacked Publius Celer fiercely
p: A Stoic teacher prosecutes the man who testified against his friend, a former governor of Asia.
b: Musonius Rufus was a Stoic philosopher. Tacitus lists him among those expelled after the Pisonian plot (Annals 15.71); Wikipedia adds the island of Gyaros, AD 65, and his return under Galba. Here he accuses Publius Celer, who had testified against Barea Soranus. Soranus was a former proconsul of Asia, charged under Nero; his daughter Servilia was summoned too, and Thrasea, Soranus and Servilia were each allowed to choose their death (Annals 16.23; 16.31; 16.33). Asia is the Roman province where Paul spent two years: "everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word" (Acts 19:10). This trial is the first test of whether the Senate will punish informers (4:40).

a: the fortieth milestone from Rome on the Appian Road
p: The road where Mucianus had a rival killed is the road Paul walked into Rome.
b: The Appian Road ran south from Rome. Paul came to Rome by it: "the brothers" "came out to meet us at Appius' Market and at Three Taverns" (Acts 28:15). Wikipedia's page on the road lists both stops among its stations. Place link only. Paul came to Rome on the same road, and years later a young man whom Mucianus feared was killed on it (the account of how he died is kept short on purpose).

a: I'll go back further to explain what caused this war
t: Josephus tells this same revolt in one paragraph
p: Josephus gives the German and Gallic revolt a few lines and no Batavians.
b: Josephus tells the revolt in War 7.4.2: "a great multitude of the Germans were in commotion... and as the Gauls in their neighborhood joined with them," they hoped to free themselves from Rome. In Whiston's translation he names "Classicus also, and Vitellius" as leaders, and Whiston's footnote reads these as Tacitus's Classicus and Civilis. He gives Cerialis one battle and Domitian a quick march that ends the matter. Link strength: strong. Both describe one event, in AD 69 to 70. Josephus adds that it happened "while Vespasian was about Alexandria, and Titus was lying at the siege of Jerusalem." Tacitus gives the causes, the camps and the campaigns that Josephus leaves out.

a: The Batavians used to live across the Rhine, as part of the Chatti.
p: The people at the heart of the revolt: Rome's auxiliaries from the mouth of the Rhine.
b: Tacitus says the Batavians gave the empire "only men and weapons," not tribute. Josephus puts the revolt "while Vespasian was about Alexandria, and Titus was lying at the siege of Jerusalem" (War 7.4.2). The surviving Histories breaks off at 5:26, before the end of the war, so Tacitus gives no peace terms. Nothing in the Bible touches the Batavians.

a: Civilis was cleverer than barbarians usually are
p: Tacitus's Latin word was borrowed from Greek. Paul uses the Greek word without insult.
b: The Latin barbari comes from Greek barbaroi, people whose speech was not Greek (or Latin). Romans used it for peoples outside the empire. Paul used the same Greek word more kindly: "I am in debt both to Greeks and to barbarians" (Romans 1:14), and in Christ no one is "Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free" (Colossians 3:11). On Malta, Luke calls the island's people barbaroi, and the site renders it "the local people" who were "kind to us beyond the ordinary" (Acts 28:2).

a: the officials made it worse with greed and wild living
t: The draft, and John's word to soldiers
p: Officials who ran the draft sold exemptions. John the Baptist warned soldiers and tax collectors about the same abuse.
b: Tacitus says the draft officials took bribes and let off old or weak men for a price. The Bible records the same kind of abuse at the edge of Roman power. Tax collectors asked John the Baptist what to do and he said, "Do not collect anything beyond the amount you have been assigned"; to soldiers he said, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:13-14). Agrees that Roman power often broke its own rules; the Bible's answer is to the person inside the system, not a call to revolt.

a: a sacred grove
t: Oaths and feasts in the grove
p: Germans met in groves. Moses told Israel to destroy such places.
b: Civilis uses a sacred grove (Latin nemus) for a feast and an oath, where drink and darkness can seal a plot. The Law told Israel to "wipe out completely all the places where the nations you are driving out served their gods: on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every leafy tree" (Deuteronomy 12:2). Background: many peoples held worship in groves, Canaanite and German alike. Civilis's oath and the "tribe's rites" (4:15) are not the Bible's idea of an oath; compare 4:41.

a: Caligula's ridiculous expedition
t: Caligula, the Rhine and the Temple
p: Tacitus mocks Caligula's Rhine trip. Josephus tells his plan to put his statue in the Temple.
b: Tacitus's Latin is Gaianarum expeditionum ludibrium, "the mockery of the Gaian campaigns"; Gaius is Caligula's name. This site's Gospels and Acts never name Caligula (a check of the site's translation finds only Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius). Josephus does: Gaius so abused his fortune "as to take himself to be a god" and "sent Petronius with an army to Jerusalem, to place his statues in the temple" (War 2.10.1). Some readers hear that plan behind the "abomination of desolation" in Mark 13; the site's Mark page sets out the dates. Link: background to the Gospels' world.

a: Quintilius Varus was killed and slavery was driven out of Germany
t: Varus: Herod's Syria and the Teutoburg Forest
p: Civilis names Varus, who lost three legions in Germany. Josephus's Varus ruled Syria when Herod died.
b: Civilis recalls Varus, who lost his army to the Germans (AD 9). Josephus names "Varus, the president of Syria" at Herod the Great's last trial of his son (War 1.31.5) and says that after Herod's death "Quintilius Varus was in that country" (War, Preface 7). Same person? Very likely. Velleius Paterculus, telling of Varus before his defeat, says he "entered this rich province a poor man, and left this poor province a rich man" and ties that to his governorship of Syria (Roman History 2.117.2, Shipley's translation). Wikipedia's article on Publius Quinctilius Varus dates the Syrian governorship to about 7 to 4 BC and holds that the Syrian governor and the commander lost in AD 9 are one man. The Bible never names him, but Joseph's dream-warning about Herod's son Archelaus (Matthew 2:19-22) falls in the years just after his governorship.

a: Many people are still alive in Gaul who were born before tribute.
p: Civilis calls Roman tax slavery. A Galilean rebel said much the same, and Jesus and Paul answered.
b: Civilis argues that paying tribute is slavery and that freedom is worth a war. A Jewish rebel argued the same in Judea at the time of the registration: Judas "prevailed with his countrymen to revolt, and said they were cowards if they would endure to pay a tax to the Romans and would after God submit to mortal men as their lords" (War 2.8.1; compare Acts 5:37 and Luke 2:1-3). Differs: Civilis speaks from nature and courage, Judas from God's rule. Jesus, asked about "the head tax to Caesar", said "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Matthew 22:17-21), and Paul: "If it is the tax, pay the tax" (Romans 13:7). Cerialis gives Rome's side at 4:74.

a: Freedom is a gift of nature even to animals that can't speak. Courage is humanity's own good, and the gods stand with the braver.
t: Do the gods stand with the braver?
p: Civilis says courage wins. Proverbs, Psalm 20 and Ecclesiastes say victory is not so simple.
b: Civilis says the gods side with courage. The Bible answers that victory belongs to the LORD, and that the best do not always win: "You may get the horse ready for the day of war, but the victory is the LORD's" (Proverbs 21:31); "These have chariots, and those have horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7); and "the race does not belong to the swift, or the battle to the warriors... For time and chance meet them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Differs. The outcome of this very speech bears Ecclesiastes out: Civilis wins at first and is losing by 4:79.

a: deserters and prisoners taught them to pile up timber in the shape of a bridge and then put wheels under it
t: Siege towers on the Rhine and at Jerusalem
p: The Germans learn siege work from Rome. Rome used the same work against Jerusalem in AD 70.
b: Tacitus describes siege machines: a wheeled tower, wicker screens, covered sheds, and the Romans' answers of catapults, fire and a hoist. The next summer Titus used Rome's own methods on Jerusalem. Josephus says he decided to "build a wall round about the whole city" so no one could slip out (War 5.12.1), and brought battering rams against the temple wall (War 6.4.1). Jesus had said, "Your enemies will put up a palisade of stakes against you. They will ring you round and press in on you from every side" (Luke 19:43). Link: background. Luke does not describe Rome's methods; he gives the shape of the siege.

a: letters were to be handed to the legions' eagle-bearers, who read them to the soldiers before the generals did
t: The eagle-bearers and the army's standards
p: Each legion had an eagle standard. After the Temple burned, Josephus says soldiers sacrificed to their standards.
b: A legion's standard was an eagle, and its bearer was the aquilifer (the Latin of this verse). Hordeonius Flaccus, trying to prove he had begged for help, let the eagle-bearers read the letters to the troops before the generals did. Tacitus says he "set up a very bad precedent," since the army then heard its news before its commanders. The Bible does not mention the eagles, but Josephus tells that after the Temple burned the Romans "brought their ensigns to the temple and set them over against its eastern gate; and there did they offer sacrifices to them" and hailed Titus (War 6.6.1). Some readers link that scene to the "abomination of desolation" standing "where he must not stand" (Mark 13:14); the site's Mark page sets out the views.

a: What in peacetime would have been called chance or nature was now called fate and a god's anger.
p: Roman soldiers call a drought a sign from the gods. Jesus and Josephus also speak of signs.
b: Tacitus, writing as an educated Roman, notes that "among the uneducated" the low Rhine was an omen that even the rivers were deserting Rome. People in every culture read the sky and the land in war. Jesus spoke of coming "great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11) and warned that "false messiahs and false prophets will rise up. They will give great signs and wonders" (Matthew 24:24). Josephus says that "a great number of false prophets" told besieged Jerusalem to wait for "miraculous signs of their deliverance" (War 6.5.2). Agrees that signs were everywhere; the Bible stresses testing them (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).

a: called by a Roman name, the Agrippinenses
p: The city of the Ubii was named after the emperor Claudius's wife. Claudius is in Acts.
b: The Ubii were Germans who sided with Rome. Tacitus says Claudius, at Agrippina's urging, planted a colony of veterans in the Ubian town where she was born (Annals 12.27). Wikipedia adds that the Ubii had founded a settlement at the site in 38 BC and that in AD 50 it became Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium; it is now Cologne. Claudius is named in Acts: Agabus foretold a famine that came "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28), and "Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome" (Acts 18:2). Link: Claudius yes; Agrippina is not named in the Bible.

a: the images of Vitellius were put back up in the camp and in the nearby Belgian cities
p: The army set up the emperor's picture in camps. A coin with Caesar's face is what Jesus held up.
b: Tacitus has the Rhine soldiers set up Vitellius's images again, "though Vitellius was already dead". At 4:62 the emperors' images are torn down when the legions yield. An emperor's image stood for his rule, in camps and on coins. Asked about the tax, Jesus said, "Let me see the coin you pay the tax with." They handed him a denarius. "Whose image is this, and whose name is written here?" "Caesar's," they answered (Matthew 22:19-21). Link: background to the imperial image behind the Gospels' tax question and, for some readers, behind Revelation's "image" of the beast (Revelation 13).

a: the grain ships were being held back by the severe winter weather
t: Winter sea, grain ships and Paul's voyage
p: Rome's grain came by sea from Africa and Egypt and stopped in winter. Paul sailed on such a ship.
b: Tacitus says the crowd's one worry in public affairs was the grain supply, and that bad winter weather held the ships back. Josephus explains why Vespasian first secured Egypt: it supplied "corn" to Rome, so holding it could starve a rival (War 4.10.5). Luke tells of the same trade: the centurion "came across a ship out of Alexandria bound for Italy" (Acts 27:6), Paul warned that sailing so late was risky (Acts 27:9-10), and the crew "made the ship lighter by dumping the wheat into the sea" (Acts 27:38). Agrees in detail about the trade; the events are different ones.

a: the allied kings
p: A king Agrippa and Queen Berenice backed Vespasian. The pair in Acts 25 and 26 is very likely the same.
b: Tacitus says the Senate thanked "the allied kings." Earlier he tells how Agrippa, "called away from Rome by secret messages from his people", was hurrying across the sea, and how "Queen Berenice" backed the cause "with no less spirit" (2:81). Same people as King Agrippa and Bernice in Acts? Very likely. Luke has "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), and Paul speaks before him (Acts 26:1). Josephus also has "king Agrippa" sail with Titus toward Rome (War 4.9.2). This is Herod Agrippa II, a Jewish king under Rome.

a: Domitian, the Caesar
p: Julius Caesar's family name became the emperor's title. In the Gospels, "Caesar" is the reigning emperor.
b: Caesar began as a family name (Julius Caesar). Augustus took it and later emperors kept it, and Tacitus uses it for the emperor's heir too: Domitian is "the Caesar," and Titus is "Titus Caesar." The Gospels and Acts use it for the ruler himself: "an order came out from Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1), "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1), "you are no Friend of Caesar" (John 19:12) and Paul's "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11). Here the word marks rank in the Flavian house: Vespasian rules, and his sons are Caesars.

a: On the first of January
t: The new year, the consuls and the Senate
p: The Roman year began on 1 January, when new consuls took office and the Senate met.
b: Tacitus dates the Senate's first meeting of the year to 1 January, the day new consuls took office. This is January AD 70, after the Capitol burned in December AD 69. Vespasian and Titus held the consulship that year while far from Rome (4:38). The Senate thanked "the legates, the armies and the allied kings", took a praetorship from one man and gave it to another, and gave Domitian the city praetorship, so that his name headed letters and edicts while Mucianus held the power. Josephus reports the same time from the other end: festival days in Rome "for Vespasian, as for their emperor" (War 4.11.4).

a: calling the gods as witnesses
t: Senators' oath, and Jesus on oaths
p: The Senate swears by the gods that no one was harmed by their help. Jesus says do not swear at all.
b: The senators swore, with the gods as witnesses, that they had not helped harm anyone and had taken no reward from others' disasters. The Law allowed oaths: "Do not swear by my name to a lie" (Leviticus 19:12). Jesus went further: "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), and James repeats it: "Let your 'Yes' mean yes and your 'No' mean no" (James 5:12). Differs. The senators call the gods as witnesses; the Law allows an oath only in the LORD's name and forbids swearing falsely by it (Leviticus 19:12), and Jesus goes further. Tacitus notes that the guilty "changed the words" of the oath in various ways. Oaths of loyalty come up again at 4:21, 4:31 and 4:59.

a: Those who outlived Tiberius and Caligula thought the same
t: The emperors the New Testament names
p: Tiberius, Caligula, Nero, Vespasian: which of them are in the Gospels and Acts?
b: Montanus lists the tyrants. This site's Gospels and Acts name three emperors: Augustus (Luke 2:1), Tiberius (Luke 3:1) and Claudius (Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2). They never name Caligula, Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian or Domitian (checked against the site's translation). Paul's appeal is to "Caesar's judgment seat" (Acts 25:10-12), which means Nero's court, though the title does not say so. The Bible's Rome is mostly nameless, and Josephus and Tacitus fill in the names.

a: sent back to the same islands
p: Rome sent condemned senators to islands. John says he was on Patmos for his testimony.
b: Mucianus sends two men back to the islands where they had been banished. Island exile was a Roman punishment; Tacitus says Nero expelled Musonius (Annals 15.71), and Wikipedia names the island of Gyaros. John writes: "I was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). Background only. John does not say Rome exiled him. Whether he was banished, as many readers hold, or went there some other way, is argued; the site's Revelation pages weigh it.

a: the people of Cyrene
p: Cyrene, a city in Libya, sent a man to carry Jesus's cross and Jews to Jerusalem.
b: Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa with Jewish residents. The Bible names it often: "Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus" carried the cross (Mark 15:21); Cyrenians had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9); "parts of Libya near Cyrene" are named at Pentecost (Acts 2:10); and Lucius the Cyrenian taught in the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1). Tacitus's trial is an extortion case: Cyrene's people complain of a Roman governor's cruelty. Josephus tells of unrest among Cyrene's Jews after the war (War 7.11.1).

a: a censor's funeral was held for Flavius Sabinus
t: Flavius Sabinus and the burning Capitol
p: Domitian honors the uncle who died when the Capitol was taken. Josephus tells the same fight.
b: Flavius Sabinus was Vespasian's brother. Josephus calls Domitian "his brother's son" and tells how Sabinus "seized upon the capitol" by night, how Vitellius's soldiers from Germany took the hill, how "Sabinus himself was brought to Vitellius, and then slain," and how Domitian "providentially escaped" while "the soldiers also plundered the temple of its ornaments, and set it on fire" (War 4.11.4). Tacitus tells the same fight in Book 3. Link strength: strong. Both put Sabinus's death at the Capitol and Domitian's escape there. Domitian, who had been in the Capitol with his uncle, now moves the honor (4:47); the Capitol's rebuilding comes at 4:53.

a: the legion and the auxiliaries in Africa, guarding the empire's borders, were under the proconsul
p: Why Rome's governors in Acts have different titles, and why Africa had two rivals.
b: A proconsul governed a province the Senate sent him to; a legate was the emperor's deputy, often with the army; a procurator was an official, often of the Knights, who ran finances and in smaller provinces governed. Tacitus tells how Caligula split Africa's command, setting a legate beside the proconsul so each distrusted the other. The Bible uses the same words of its governors. "The proconsul Sergius Paulus" (Acts 13:7), "Gallio... proconsul of Achaia" (Acts 18:12) and "there are proconsuls" (Acts 19:38) are senators' posts. Judea's governors were of the other kind: Josephus says Coponius "was sent as a procurator" and Pilate "was sent as procurator into Judea by Tiberius" (War 2.8.1; 2.9.2), though Luke says only that Pilate "was governing Judea" (Luke 3:1).

a: Valerius Festus commanded the legion in Africa, a young man of extravagant habits and wild ambition
p: Two Roman officers named Festus. The one in Acts 24 to 26 is a different man. Not the same person.
b: The Festus of Acts is "Porcius Festus," who "took over from Felix" as governor of Judea and heard Paul (Acts 24:27; Acts 25:10-12). Tacitus's Festus is Valerius Festus, legate of the legion in Africa in AD 69 to 70, and Tacitus calls him "a young man." Same person? No. The family names differ, the posts differ, and Paul stood before Porcius Festus years before AD 70, while Tacitus calls Valerius Festus a young man in AD 70.

a: one of the procurators of Africa
p: A procurator was a Roman finance officer. Judea had one in Pilate's day.
b: Tacitus uses the Latin procurator, an officer who handled the emperor's money and, in some provinces, governed. Baebius Massa held one of the posts in Africa. The title is the one Josephus gives to the men who governed Judea before the war (see the note at 4:48). Tacitus calls Massa's name "already deadly to good men" and a name that will "come back among the causes of the troubles we soon suffered," a promise the surviving text does not reach: it stops at 5:26.

a: finish what was left of the Jewish war
p: Vespasian gives Titus the army that will besiege Jerusalem. Jesus had spoken of that siege.
b: Josephus agrees: once Vespasian had set Alexandria in order he "sent his son Titus, with a select part of his army, to destroy Jerusalem" (War 4.11.5), and he lists Titus's march by Pelusium and Gaza to Caesarea. The siege that followed is what Jesus foretold: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20), and "here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Matthew 24:2). Josephus dates the temple's burning to the tenth of Lous (Whiston adds "Ab" in brackets), "upon which it was formerly burnt by the king of Babylon" (War 6.4.5). The Bible does not name Titus. Same person as Paul's Titus? No. Paul's Titus was "a Greek" convert (Galatians 2:3) and "my partner and my fellow worker" (2 Corinthians 8:23); this Titus was Vespasian's son.
r: Luke 19:43-44; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 24:2; Galatians 2:1-3; 2 Corinthians 8:23; Titus 1:4

a: Envoys of King Vologesus were there, offering forty thousand Parthian horsemen
p: Parthia, Rome's great rival to the east, is named at Pentecost.
b: Vologesus ruled Parthia, the empire east of Rome. Vespasian thanks him and turns the offer down, "proud and glad to be courted" but not in need. Parthians are in the Bible's first Christian crowd: "We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites" (Acts 2:9). Link: background to Acts.

a: Even brothers won't keep up harmony unless the parent sets the example.
p: Titus begs for Domitian. Suetonius says Domitian later plotted against Titus.
b: Titus argues that a large family is a surer defense than legions. The ancient picture is bitter. Suetonius says Domitian, after his father died, claimed a share of power and said the will had been tampered with, and that he plotted against Titus until Titus's last illness (Domitian 2.3). The Bible praises the harmony Titus wants: "Look how good it is, how lovely, when brothers live together, all as one!" (Psalm 133:1). Brothers at odds fill its stories too, from Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:8) to Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27:41) to Joseph's brothers (Genesis 37:4).

a: no more than ten days' grain in the storehouses
p: Rome had ten days of grain left. Acts 11 tells of a famine in Claudius's day.
b: Tacitus says the city stood ten days from empty storehouses until Vespasian's ships came. Rome fed on imported grain, and Josephus says Vespasian took Egypt first because of it (War 4.10.5). Hunger is a thread in Acts too: Agabus "indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was going to strike the whole inhabited world. It did come, in the days of Claudius," and the disciples at Antioch sent aid to Judea (Acts 11:28-30). Link: the same world of grain and shortage, not the same famine.

a: He gave the job of rebuilding the Capitol to Lucius Vestinius
p: Rome rebuilds Jupiter's temple the year Jerusalem's temple burns. Ezra and Haggai tell a rebuilding too.
b: The Capitol, Rome's temple of Jupiter, burned in the fighting for Rome (Tacitus 3:71-3:72); Wikipedia gives the day, 19 December AD 69, and says it was rebuilt on the same foundations and dedicated in AD 75. Suetonius says Vespasian "carried some of it off on his own head" while clearing the rubble (Vespasian 8.5). In AD 70 Jerusalem's temple burned, and Josephus says the Jews' yearly temple payment was redirected: "two drachmae every year into the Capitol, as they used to pay the same to the temple at Jerusalem" (War 7.6.6; Dio 65.7). That is the "double drachma" of Matthew 17:24. The Bible has its own rebuilding: when the foundation was laid, old men "wept out loud" (Ezra 3:12), and Haggai promised, "The last glory of this house will be greater than the first" (Haggai 2:9). Differs: Rome's priests insist on the old footprint; Haggai's house is for the LORD, and the Bible places it on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1).

a: The soothsayers he called together
t: Haruspices, Vestals and the three-animal rite
p: Roman specialists read entrails, and the site was purified with a pig, a sheep and a bull.
b: The soothsayers are haruspices, specialists who read signs in the entrails of sacrificed animals. The "Vestal Virgins" washed the site, and Helvidius, with a pontiff reciting the words, purified it with a pig, a sheep and a bull (Latin suovetaurilia). The Law has no pig offering: "The pig... is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7), and Isaiah lists "pig's blood" among the offerings the LORD rejects (Isaiah 66:3). Differs: the Roman rite is built for a god who must be pleased by the correct form, which is why the soothsayers forbid changing the footprint. The Bible's temple rites are given by the LORD in the Law (see the topic Sacrifice and Offerings).

a: said the Druids with the empty superstition of prophets
t: Druids' prophecy, tested by the Bible's test
p: The Druids read the Capitol fire as the end of Rome. The Bible gives a test for prophecies.
b: The Gauls took the burning of Jupiter's Capitol as a sign that rule would pass to peoples "beyond the Alps." Tacitus calls it "empty superstition" (superstitione vana). The Bible's test for a prophet: "When the prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the thing does not happen or come true, that is a word the LORD has not spoken" (Deuteronomy 18:22). The Druids do not speak in the LORD's name, so the test is not strictly theirs, but the principle fits: events 4:71-4:78 show the Druids' word failed. Josephus describes false prophets inside Jerusalem who said deliverance was coming (War 6.5.2). Agrees with Tacitus that signs can mislead, though for Tacitus the cure is education and for the Bible it is God's word.

a: the winter camps in Moesia and Pannonia were besieged by the Sarmatae and Dacians
t: Sarmatians on the Danube: Tacitus and Josephus
p: Tacitus calls the rumor false. Josephus records a real Sarmatian raid into Moesia in the same year.
b: Tacitus says the Gauls heard a false rumor of Sarmatians and Dacians besieging camps on the Danube. Josephus says the Scythians "who are called Sarmatians" really did cross the Danube into Moesia, killing "the consular legate Fonteius Agrippa," until Rubrius Gallus drove them back (War 7.4.3). Tacitus names Fonteius Agrippa as Moesia's new governor at 3:46. Link strength: strong, with a difference. Tacitus's "false" is about a siege of winter camps, Josephus's raid happened at "the very same time" as the German revolt. Two Bible place names belong to the same Danube lands: Paul preached "as far as Illyricum" (Romans 15:19) and Titus went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10).

a: Now, said the Druids with the empty superstition of prophets, the deadly fire was a sign of heaven's anger
t: Two sanctuaries on fire in one year
p: Claude's theory: Gauls and Jews both read a burning sanctuary as heaven's verdict. Only one read it before it happened.
b: Claude's reading: AD 70 gives two burning sanctuaries and two readings. The Druids read the Capitol fire (December AD 69) as heaven's anger on Rome. Josephus reads the Temple's fire (August AD 70) as an old doom: "God had, for certain, long ago doomed it to the fire" (War 6.4.5). The difference is when the word was spoken. Jesus said of the Temple, "here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Matthew 24:2), about forty years before it happened. The Druids' word came after the fire and was false by 4:79.

a: the divine Julius
p: Rome made dead emperors gods. Acts shows a crowd calling a living king a god.
b: Rome called deified rulers divus, "divine"; Julius Caesar was the first. Sabinus said his great-grandmother had caught Julius's eye in Gaul, claiming descent from him. Dio notes the claim too (65.3). The Bible meets ruler worship: when Herod spoke, "the crowd kept crying out, 'It's a god speaking, not a man!'", and "an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God" (Acts 12:22-23). In Revelation the beast is worshiped (Revelation 13:4). Differs: Rome made emperors gods by decree; the Bible says no human may take the glory.

a: You, Jupiter, best and greatest
p: Vocula prays to Jupiter, the god of the burned Capitol. Lystra took Barnabas for Zeus.
b: Vocula prays to Jupiter Best and Greatest (Latin Iuppiter optime maxime), whose temple was the Capitol (4:53), and to Quirinus, whom he calls father of the city. Jupiter is the Roman Zeus. At Lystra, "They named Barnabas 'Zeus,'" and "the priest of Zeus... brought bulls and wreaths of flowers to the gates" (Acts 14:12-13). Paul answered, "turn from these empty things to the God who lives" (Acts 14:15). Differs: the Bible calls such gods empty (Psalm 115:4-8; Isaiah 44:9-10) and, in Paul's words, what is sacrificed to them goes "to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20; compare Deuteronomy 32:17). Christian readers weigh these two lines, empty and demonic, as the topic The Divine Council shows.

a: they pulled up shrubs, roots and the grass growing between stones
p: The starving camp at the Old Camp is like Samaria and Jerusalem under siege.
b: Tacitus keeps his picture of the starving camp short. The Bible has other sieges: in Samaria "the siege went on until the price of a donkey's head was eighty pieces of silver" (2 Kings 6:25). Jesus foretold Jerusalem's siege (Luke 21:20-24), and Josephus describes the famine inside the city in AD 70 (War 5.10.2-3). Agrees that besieged people eat what the law and custom forbid, and that hunger, more than the sword, ends sieges. (The Law's list of unclean animals is in Leviticus 11.)

a: Civilis fulfilled a vow of the kind barbarians make
p: Civilis keeps his hair long until the vow is done, like a Nazirite. Acts 18:18 has a hair-cut for a vow.
b: Civilis let his hair grow and dyed it red until the legions were destroyed, then cut it off. The Law's Nazirite did something like it: when the vow was over, "the Nazirite will shave off the hair he dedicated. He will take that hair and throw it into the fire burning under the peace offering" (Numbers 6:18). Acts 18:18 says that someone, Paul or Aquila, "had had his hair cut short at Cenchreae, for he was keeping a vow"; the Greek participle keiramenos follows the names Priscilla and Aquila and can go with either man. Parallel in form, no link. Civilis's vow is to himself and to war; the Nazirite's vow is to the LORD and ends in an offering. Tacitus says hair-vows are what "barbarians" do, which the Bible shows is not only a German practice.

a: She was a maiden of the Bructeri tribe who ruled a wide territory.
p: A German woman prophet whom some worshiped. The Bible has prophetesses and refuses worship.
b: Tacitus says the Germans treated many women as prophets and, as belief grew, as goddesses. Veleda's authority was highest after she predicted the German victory and the legions' end. Wikipedia says her name probably means "seeress." The Bible has women who spoke for God: "Deborah, a woman and a prophet" judged Israel (Judges 4:4), Anna "a prophetess" met the child Jesus (Luke 2:36), and Philip had four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:8-9); Miriam is called "the prophet" (Exodus 15:20). Differs on worship. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes when a crowd treats them as gods (Acts 14:14-15). Veleda is sent a Roman legate among the gifts. Compare 4:65.

a: It was also reported that he handed over some of the prisoners to his small son to shoot with a child's arrows and javelins.
p: Tacitus signals a rumor with ferebatur. He does not say it was true.
b: The Latin ferebatur means "it was being said." Here Tacitus does not vouch for the story, as he does not at 4:49, where he writes incertum, "unclear," about what Piso and Festus said in private. The reader should hold the sentence as a report about a man who had just destroyed Roman legions, told by a Roman. It is one plain sentence and is kept short in these notes.

a: How he hid and stayed alive for nine years, his friends' steady loyalty, and the fine example of his wife Epponina, I'll tell in the right place.
t: Sabinus in hiding for nine years
p: Tacitus promises the story of Sabinus's nine years. The surviving text stops before it.
b: Julius Sabinus ran from his defeat and let it be said he had burned himself in a house. Dio says he hid in a vault for nine years and had two sons there, and that he claimed descent from Julius Caesar (Dio 65.3). Tacitus promises the full story "in the right place", but the surviving Histories ends at 5:26, before it. Link strength: partial. Dio gives the nine years and the claim to descent that Tacitus gives at 4:55; Of the two, only Tacitus names the wife (Epponina, 4:67); Dio says only "his wife". Nothing in the Bible touches him.

a: That was the state of the war when Petilius Cerialis reached Mogontiacum.
p: Three ancient writers tell how Cerialis ended the revolt. They differ on where he came from.
b: Tacitus has Mucianus choose Cerialis (4:68) and follows his campaign from Mogontiacum to the Treveri. Josephus says Vespasian made Cerialis consul, sent him to Britain, and that when he heard of the Germans' revolt "he fell upon them as soon as they were gotten together, and put his army in battle-array, and slew a great number of them" (War 7.4.2). Dio says Cerialis ended the uprisings in battles after which a river was dammed by the dead (65.3). Link strength: strong. All three agree on the man and the result. They differ on who sent him and from where; Tacitus gives the detail that Josephus and Dio leave out.

a: Put up with the extravagance or greed of your rulers the way you put up with barren seasons, too much rain and other natural evils.
p: Cerialis tells Gauls to bear bad rulers like bad weather. Paul calls rulers God's servants for good.
b: Cerialis says rulers' vices are like droughts: nobody can stop them. Paul gives a reason, and a limit: "Rulers are not something to fear for those who do good, but for those who do evil" (Romans 13:3); the ruler "is God's servant, there for your good" (Romans 13:4). A prophet speaks the other side: "Woe to those who lay down wicked rules, and to the scribes who keep writing up misery" (Isaiah 10:1). Differs: for Cerialis the ruler is a fact of nature; for the Bible he is answerable to God, who also hears the poor.

a: no peace among nations without armies, no armies without pay, and no pay without taxes
p: Cerialis defends Roman taxes. Paul told believers to pay them, and John told soldiers to be content with their pay.
b: Cerialis is Rome's spokesman: taxes buy peace, and Gauls share in the empire. Paul accepted part of this: "This is also why you pay taxes. The authorities are God's public servants" (Romans 13:6). John told soldiers, "Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14). Civilis made the opposite speech at 4:17. The Bible gives no ruling that taxes are always just; it asks believers to pay what is owed and to keep from dishonest gain.

a: In those months while Vespasian waited at Alexandria for the regular days of the summer winds and a dependable sea
p: Why the new emperor was in Egypt, and what Josephus says he did there.
b: Egypt was the key to Rome's grain, so Vespasian took it first. Josephus tells how he wrote to Tiberius Alexander, "then governor of Egypt and of Alexandria," who had the legions swear to him (War 4.10.6). Alexandria was "the greatest of all cities next to Rome," and when news of Vitellius's end came there, Vespasian sent Titus on to Jerusalem and himself prepared to sail for Rome (War 4.11.5). Josephus says nothing about healings or the temple of Serapis. This same Tiberius Alexander had put down an Alexandrian Jewish rising earlier as governor of the city, and "fifty thousand" Jews lay dead (War 2.18.7-8).
r: Josephus, War 4.10.5-6; Josephus, War 4.11.5; Josephus, War 2.18.7-8; Acts 6:9

a: He begged the emperor to deign to wet his cheeks and the rims of his eyes with spit from his mouth.
t: Spit and sight: Alexandria and Bethsaida
p: A blind man is healed with spit on his eyes at Alexandria. Mark tells of a blind man healed with spit at Bethsaida.
b: At Alexandria the blind man asks for spit on his eyes. In Mark, Jesus "spat into the man's eyes, placed his hands on him and asked, 'Is there anything you can see?'" (Mark 8:23); he also used spit with a deaf man (Mark 7:33) and in clay on a blind man's eyes (John 9:6). Suetonius (Vespasian 7.2-3) and Dio (65.8) tell the Alexandria story too. Eric Eve argues that Mark added the spit to the Bethsaida story to allude to Vespasian's and set Jesus's messiahship against Rome's (New Testament Studies 54, 2008). That needs a Mark written after AD 69; the site's Mark page lists dates from the early 40s to about 75. Differs: Jesus is not asked by an oracle, Mark shows no doctor's opinion asked, and Jesus takes the man outside the village and sends him home without letting him back into it (Mark 8:23; Mark 8:26). Whether the Gospel stories answer Rome's is argued; that each stands on witnesses of its own is the Christian reading.

a: Another man, sick in the hand, on the authority of the same god, asked that it be stepped on by the emperor's foot.
p: A damaged hand in Alexandria, and a withered hand in two Gospels.
b: Tacitus's second petitioner has a hand that is "sick"; Suetonius has a lame leg and a touch of the heel (7.2); Dio, in the Loeb English, a withered hand cured by treading (65.8). Mark and Matthew tell of a man "whose hand had withered" in a synagogue, healed by a word: "Stretch out your hand. He stretched it out, and his hand was made well again" (Mark 3:1-5; Matthew 12:9-13). The Bible has other public cures of damaged limbs: the lame man at the Beautiful Gate, whose healing the rulers could not deny (Acts 3:1-10; Acts 4:16), and a lame man at Lystra, after which the crowds named Barnabas "Zeus" (Acts 14:8-12). Differs: the Alexandrian cure uses a foot on the hand and ends with applause for the emperor. Jesus's cure comes in a Sabbath dispute and ends with his opponents plotting (Mark 3:6).

a: he ordered the doctors to judge whether such blindness and weakness could be overcome by human help
p: Vespasian asks doctors if the cures are possible. The Gospels also mention doctors who failed.
b: Vespasian asks doctors before he acts, and the doctors weigh in: the eyes' power of sight "hadn't been eaten away," the bent joints "could be made whole if a healing force were applied," and "the glory of a cure would belong to the emperor, and the ridicule of failure to the poor sufferers." The Gospels show doctors in a different light: the woman "had spent every penny she owned" on them and "had only gotten worse" (Mark 5:26; Luke 8:43), and Jesus quotes the proverb "Doctor, cure yourself!" (Luke 4:23). Differs. Vespasian's doctors give him a safe way out if the cure fails. In the Gospels and Acts the critics examine a cure and cannot deny it (John 9:30-33; Acts 4:16).

a: thinking that everything lay open to his fortune and that nothing was beyond belief now
t: Healing as politics: how scholars read it
p: Meier and Dickson call it a staged show; Eve calls it Flavian propaganda; Tacitus gives the doctors' view.
b: Tacitus gives Vespasian's own motive: "everything lay open to his fortune." John Meier, as quoted by John Dickson, writes that Vespasian lacked a clear claim to the throne and "there is nothing like a miracle story to give one indisputable legitimacy", and calls it a "photo opportunity"; Dickson concludes the story is probably a fraud. Eric Eve reads it as Flavian propaganda for a new claimant. Suetonius says Vespasian "had hardly any faith that this could possibly succeed" (Vespasian 7.3). Beside the Roman telling itself, three readings are open: staged, an ordinary recovery (Tacitus's doctors think the sight was not destroyed), or a sign with a source beyond the emperor. The third is a Christian reading, and no named holder is cited for it here; it rests on the Bible's own tests of signs: Matthew 24:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2:9 warn that "signs and wonders" can serve falsehood, while Deuteronomy 13:1-3 says to test a sign by what it asks you to worship.

a: Those who were present still tell of both, now that there is nothing to gain from lying.
p: Tacitus leans on living witnesses. Paul and Luke do the same, with a different cost to the witness.
b: Tacitus argues that the witnesses have nothing to gain from lying, since the Flavian emperors can no longer reward them. Luke opens his Gospel by pointing to "the people who saw it with their own eyes from the beginning" (Luke 1:2), and Paul says of the risen Christ that "more than five hundred brothers" saw him at one time, "Most of them are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6). The Sanhedrin could say nothing against a man healed in plain view (Acts 4:14; Acts 4:16). Agrees that living witnesses carry weight. The cost differs: Vespasian's witnesses had nothing to gain by lying, the apostles were whipped for the name (Acts 5:40-41).

a: this people, devoted to many superstitions
p: Tacitus's word for foreign or excessive religion. Paul calls Athens very devoted to the gods.
b: The Latin superstitio is Tacitus's word for religion he finds excessive or foreign. He uses it of the Egyptians here, of the Druids (4:54), of German prophetesses (4:61), of the Jews (5:8; 5:13). It is a judgment, not a neutral word. Luke has Paul say to Athens, "I see how very devoted to the gods you are, in every way" (Acts 17:22). The site's Greek word list glosses the word there as "very religious."

a: and daylight shone again for the blind man
t: A pair of cures: eyes and a limb
p: Claude's theory: sight and a damaged limb together are what Isaiah 35 and Jesus's answer to John list.
b: Claude's reading: Tacitus pairs two cures (sight, and a limb). Isaiah promised that on God's day "blind people's eyes will open" and "a lame man will jump like a deer" (Isaiah 35:5-6), and Jesus answered John, "The blind see again and the lame walk" (Matthew 11:5). Eyes and limbs are common ailments, so the pair may be chance. But if Eve is right that Mark answered the Alexandria story, a first-century Jewish or Christian hearer might also have heard Matthew 11:5 against it.

a: one of the leading Egyptians, named Basilides
p: Vespasian reads his answer from a name. Basilides is built on Greek basileus, king.
b: Tacitus says Vespasian "read the force of the response from the name Basilides". The name comes from Greek basileus, "king", and it was heard as the god's word that Vespasian would be king. Suetonius also has a Basilides but makes him a freedman who "offered him sacred boughs, garlands, and loaves" (Vespasian 7.1). The Greek word basileus is the New Testament's word for king: "Where is the newborn king of the Jews?" (Matthew 2:2) and "another king" (Acts 17:7). Rome heard "king" as a promise to Vespasian; the Gospels use it of Jesus.

a: He went in and was concentrating on the god when he looked back
t: Vespasian asks the god about the empire
p: A Jewish prisoner had told him years before that he would be emperor. Tacitus and Suetonius know the story.
b: Vespasian goes alone into the temple to ask about the empire. Josephus says that after Jotapata fell, as a captive, he told Vespasian: "Thou, O Vespasian, art Caesar and emperor, thou, and this thy son" (War 3.8.9). Suetonius (Vespasian 5.6) and Dio (65.1) both report that prediction. Tacitus says elsewhere that most people there were convinced that their priests' ancient writings promised rule to men from Judea: "Those riddles had really predicted Vespasian and Titus" (5:13); Suetonius says an "old and established belief" spread across the East (Vespasian 4.5). Josephus reads the same oracle as Vespasian's (War 6.5.4). Link strength: strong for the oracle; Josephus is the source for his own role, which Tacitus here does not mention.

a: The Egyptian priests tell it this way.
p: Plutarch tells how Serapis came from Sinope too. The core agrees, the details differ.
b: Plutarch tells it of the first Ptolemy (Soter): he saw in a dream a colossal statue of Pluto at Sinope, a traveler named Sosibius said he had seen such a statue there, and Soteles and Dionysius took it from Sinope to Egypt after a long effort. Timotheus, an expounder of sacred law, and Manetho of Sebennytus, basing their guess on the Cerberus and the serpent with the statue, persuaded Ptolemy that it was the image of Serapis (On Isis and Osiris 28, in the Perseus English text, which does not name its translator). Link strength: strong. Tacitus and Plutarch share the dream, Sinope and Timotheus. Tacitus adds King Scydrothemis, the answer of the Pythian Apollo, the three years and the voyage in three days.

a: In a dream a youth appeared to him
p: A king dreams a god's order and Egypt's priests cannot read it. Pharaoh's magicians failed too.
b: Ptolemy's priests "knew little of Pontus or foreign lands," so a Greek, Timotheus, reads the dream. Pharaoh also dreamed: he "sent for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men... but not one of them could interpret it" until Joseph said, "God has told Pharaoh what he is about to do" (Genesis 41:8; Genesis 41:25). Differs: the Bible's dreams have one source and are read by the one God who gave them. In Matthew, Joseph is warned in a dream to take the child "to Egypt" (Matthew 2:13) and, after Herod's death, to go back (Matthew 2:19-20).

a: newly founded Alexandria
p: The city founded by Alexander where Jews, Greeks and Egyptians lived together.
b: In Tacitus 4:83 the first Ptolemy is shown adding walls, temples and rites to the newly founded city. The Bible knows the city: Alexandrians had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), "Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth" taught at Ephesus (Acts 18:24), and Paul sailed to Rome on two ships out of Alexandria (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11). Josephus calls it "the greatest of all cities next to Rome" (War 4.11.5) and describes its Jewish quarter (War 2.18.7-8). The Greek Old Testament was made there. This is the setting for the healing of 4:81.

a: send his most trusted friends to Pontus
p: The statue comes from Pontus. Pontus is in Acts and 1 Peter.
b: Ptolemy's dream sends envoys to Pontus on the Black Sea. Pontus is a Bible place: Jews from "Pontus and Asia" were at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), Aquila was "a man of Pontus by birth" (Acts 18:2), and Peter writes to the "temporary residents of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1). Sinope itself is not named in the Bible. Link: place only.

a: Pythian Apollo
t: The Pythian Apollo and the Python spirit
p: The oracle god is called Pythian. Luke uses the same word for a slave girl's spirit.
b: Tacitus calls the oracle god the Pythian Apollo (Latin Pythicum Apollinem). Luke's slave girl at Philippi "had a Python spirit, and her fortune-telling earned a lot of money for her masters" (Acts 16:16), and Paul cast it out. Link: the shared word only. Tacitus's kings consult oracles for orders. The Bible forbids this (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; see the topic Sorcery and Divination), and Acts shows an oracle-spirit as something to be driven out, not obeyed.

a: The more widely told story says that the god himself boarded the ships that had been brought up to the shore, of his own will.
t: A statue that comes by itself
p: A statue boards a ship by itself. The Bible mocks idols; Ephesus had an image said to have fallen from the sky.
b: The popular version says Serapis crossed the sea by his own will. Acts also has a city that claims a divinely delivered image: at Ephesus the city clerk says Ephesus guards "the great Artemis, and of what fell from the sky" (Acts 19:35). The Bible's view of such images is that people make them and they cannot move or see: "A mouth they have, but they cannot speak... With their feet they cannot walk" (Psalm 115:5-7); Isaiah 44:9-20 describes the craftsman. Differs. Tacitus himself calls this the "most popular account," and adds that others differ.

a: Many identify the god himself with Aesculapius, because he cures sick bodies
p: Healer, underworld king, Osiris or Jupiter. Serapis was many gods at once.
b: Tacitus gives rival origins (Seleucia in Syria or Memphis) and four identifications: Aesculapius, the healing god, "because he cures sick bodies"; Osiris, "the oldest god of those peoples"; Jupiter, ruler of all; and Pluto, "going by the emblems visible on his statue." Plutarch's version of the story also ends with the statue taken to be Serapis (On Isis and Osiris 28). The link with healing is why the sick turned to him (4:81).

a: Domitian himself could stay near Lugdunum and show the strength and prestige of imperial power from close by
t: Domitian's Gaul campaign: Tacitus, Josephus and Suetonius
p: Josephus has Domitian win Gaul. Tacitus and Suetonius say he never got that far.
b: Tacitus has Mucianus hold Domitian back at Lugdunum, so that Cerialis wins the glory. Josephus tells it differently: Domitian "marched against the barbarians immediately," they "submitted themselves to him with fear," and he "returned to Rome with honor and glory" (War 7.4.2). Suetonius says Domitian planned an "uncalled for" campaign against Gaul and the Germanies to match his brother, and his father's friends talked him out of it (Domitian 2.1). Whiston's footnote suggests Josephus wrote kindly because Domitian was one of his patrons. Link strength: strong, and the accounts conflict. Tacitus and Suetonius agree that Domitian did not take the field; Josephus stands alone.

a: He pretended to love literature and poetry
p: Tacitus and Suetonius agree: Domitian used poetry as a mask.
b: Suetonius says Domitian feigned modesty and an interest in poetry, which had been strange to him before, and gave public readings (Domitian 2.2). Tacitus has the same picture with a cause: to hide his mind from his brother's jealous eye. The two ancient writers agree, and some readers place the later Domitian behind Revelation's picture of a ruler who is worshiped (Revelation 13:4); the date is argued on the site's Revelation pages.
